Headteacher’s Welcome
At the forefront of education for more than a century, Upton Court Grammar School successfully blends tradition with a forward-thinking, internationally-minded educational philosophy that truly meets the needs of young people venturing into adulthood in an increasingly complex world.
Our Mission Statement is Upton Court Grammar School ensured all students fulfilled their academic and personal aspirations and thrived as successful and engaged citizens.
We believe achieving academic qualifications is important but also look to develop personal qualities like leadership and teamwork, determination and flexibility, respect and consideration, confidence and self-belief. At UCGS, we support students to achieve an extremely high level academically whilst allowing them to develop as a whole person through nurturing and valuing these non-academic skills. As a selective school, we provide academic young people from all backgrounds with the means to compete in the challenging future labour market and become principled and active citizens.
Education at Upton Court Grammar School is about inspirational teachers and aspirational pupils based firmly on high expectations and our behaviours at school are values-driven. Our core UCGS values of Unity, Curiosity, Growth and Service serve as an internal barometer for staff and students when making decisions and choices. Our core values can be seen in our culture, our routines, our behaviours and our relationships. We expect nothing but the best from our students who continue to reward our trust with excellent examination results, sought after university offers and exceptional levels of participation in extracurricular and enrichment activities. Our results speak for themselves and have been validated by an Ofsted inspection grading of Outstanding in every category.
Upton Court is a successful school community built on a strong culture and curriculum which takes into account the richness and diversity brought in by all members of our community. As a world class school we take our commitment to the wider community very seriously and expect our parents to be active participants. I know I can count on every single member of the school community’s support to fulfil one simple aim:
Ad astra (reach for the stars)
If you share this vision and want your child to be part of it, I look forward to working with you.
Mr O King MChem PGCE NPQHHeadteacherUpton Court Grammar SchoolFounded 1912

Careers
Careers, Education, Advice and Guidance at UCGS
Upton Court Grammar School ensured that all students fulfilled their academic and personal aspirations and thrived as successful and engaged citizens.
Our careers programme, in addition to our academic and pastoral programmes, will support students to achieve the school’s mission through high quality careers education and guidance that equips them with the skills, knowledge and understanding to plan and manage their careers effectively. Our mission is aligned with the CDI’s Career Development Framework which clarifies the skills, knowledge and attitudes that individuals need to have a positive career. We want to support students to thrive on an intrapersonal, interpersonal, societal and global level and be happy with the way they spend their time, being able to make a positive contribution to their communities and being able to have a decent standard of living.
As a school, with a high ability intake, we tailor our advice and guidance towards A-Level and degree level study whilst still promoting different pathways at 16 and 18 such as apprenticeships, T-Levels, and entrepreneurship. We promote equality of opportunity, celebrate diversity and challenge stereotypes to inspire and motivate students towards competitive courses at elite universities.

Who is responsible for careers education, information, advice and guidance (CEIAG)?
Mr Navroop Sehmi (Head of Careers) manages the implementation of the CEIAG programme.
In addition, a range of people contribute to achieving the aims of the programme. These include: school governors, the senior leadership team, subject teams, pastoral teams, external agencies such as Slough Borough Council, Berkshire Careers Hub and parents.
Email: NSehmi@uptoncourtgrammar.org.uk
We are committed to providing our students with a careers programme that meets all the 8 Gatsby benchmarks (GB). Our programme is delivered through a combination of methods including through our pastoral programme as well as special events.
The curriculum for Careers is embedded through our use of Unifrog – The universal destinations platform (link here). Each Year group from 7 to 13, will be guided through 6 distinct phases throughout the academic year:
Phase 1 – Grow throughout life (GB2/GB3/GB8)
Grow throughout life by learning and reflecting on yourself, your background, and your strengths.
This learning area develops students’ self-awareness and their ability to continue learning and developing throughout their lives. Students learn to seek and respond positively to help, support and feedback; recognise the value of challenging themselves; and reflect on their achievements, experiences, skills and qualifications. As they progress through the year groups, they take increasing responsibility for their learning, communicate their strengths and achievements to others, and plan their next steps in education and work. They also consider how their heritage, identity and personal values shape who they are and influence the decisions they make.
Phase 2 – Explore possibilities (GB2/GB7)
Explore the full range of possibilities open to you and learn about recruitment processes and the culture of different workplaces.
This learning area broadens students’ understanding of the opportunities available within education, training and employment. Students begin by exploring different jobs, employment sectors, organisations and learning pathways before developing the skills needed to research qualifications, entry requirements, workplaces and labour-market information. They also learn how recruitment and selection processes operate, including the purpose of CVs, applications, interviews and assessment activities. By the end of the programme, students should be able to compare different pathways and workplaces, identify the requirements of careers that interest them, and prepare effectively to access and succeed in their chosen opportunities.
Phase 3 – Manage Career (GB2/GB7/GB8)
Manage your career actively, make the most of opportunities and learn from setbacks.
This learning area helps students understand that a career is an ongoing journey through life, learning and work rather than a single job or fixed destination. Students are encouraged to imagine different possible futures, consider the challenges, risks and rewards associated with different pathways, and make informed decisions about their next steps. As they progress, they develop the confidence to set goals, prioritise actions and create realistic plans for transitions such as choosing GCSE subjects, selecting post-16 or post-18 pathways, and moving into employment or further study. The area also develops resilience by helping students anticipate, respond to and learn from challenges, setbacks and changes in circumstances.
Phase 4 – Create opportunities (GB2/GB6/GB7)
Create opportunities by being proactive and building positive relationships with others.
This learning area encourages students to take an active role in creating and pursuing opportunities for themselves and others. Students learn about the importance of positive relationships, communication, initiative, creativity and flexibility when developing their career pathways. They progress from identifying role models and understanding entrepreneurship to building networks, seeking work experience, volunteering or paid employment, and representing themselves confidently in professional settings. The learning area also develops leadership and self-advocacy, encouraging students to take responsibility for making things happen, adapt their plans when necessary, and consider entrepreneurship, freelance work and self-employment as possible career pathways.
Phase 5 – Balance life and work (GB2/GB3/GB6/GB7)
Balance your life as a worker and/or entrepreneur with your wellbeing, other interests and your involvement with your family and community.
This learning area supports students in considering how work fits alongside their wellbeing, relationships, responsibilities and wider life goals. Students explore work–life balance, physical and mental wellbeing, personal definitions of success, financial management, and the different roles people may have within their families and communities. As they become older, they consider the financial implications of education, employment, apprenticeships, higher education, self-employment and different life stages. They also develop an understanding of workplace rights and responsibilities and learn to recognise and challenge prejudice, stereotyping and discrimination in education and employment.
Phase 6 – See the big picture (GB2/GB3/GB6)
See the big picture by paying attention to how the economy, politics and society connect with your own life and career.
This learning area helps students understand that career decisions and employment opportunities are influenced by wider social, economic, political, technological and environmental factors. Students learn to evaluate different media, information sources and viewpoints, identify labour-market trends, and consider how developments such as artificial intelligence, remote working and changing working patterns may affect future jobs. They also explore how careers and employers affect communities, society and the natural environment. As they progress, students are encouraged not only to recognise these wider influences but also to respond to them when evaluating employers, researching opportunities and making informed decisions about their own futures.

Special Educational Needs & Disabilities (SEND)
Upton Court Grammar School (UCGS) is committed to ensuring that every student, including those with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND), achieves their academic and personal aspirations and thrives as a successful, engaged citizen. We value the diverse abilities and achievements of all our students and strive to provide an optimal environment for teaching and learning—supporting success socially, emotionally, and academically.
Policy and Practice Updates (2026–27)
SEND is now a core focus in school inspections: The new Ofsted framework (February 2025) places SEND as a standalone category in school evaluations. SEND provision at UCGS is central to our school improvement planning, staff training, and curriculum adaptations.
Graduated Approach: We follow the ‘Assess, Plan, Do, Review’ cycle to ensure that support is tailored, monitored, and regularly reviewed for each student.
Pupil Passports: All students with SEND have a Pupil Passport, co-produced with the student and their family, outlining needs, strategies, and targets. These are reviewed regularly.
Access Arrangements: We provide reasonable adjustments and access arrangements for both the curriculum and examinations, as required, ensuring that these reflect each students individual needs and normal way of working.
Staff Training: Ongoing SEND-specific training is delivered to all staff, including input from external specialists (e.g., Berkshire Sensory Consortium and the Local Authority).
Facilities: The school is fully accessible, with ramps, lifts, accessible toilets, and a dedicated medical/therapy space. The ZEN Room is a safe and supportive space where students can access individual and group interventions tailored to their needs.
Inclusion and Support
Holistic Support: Our SEND team (SENDCo, three Teaching Assistants, and Assistant Head for Student Welfare) works with individuals and small groups to foster a positive learning environment. We support a wide range of needs, including physical, sensory, cognitive, communication, social, emotional, and behavioural needs.
Collaboration: We work closely with students, families, teaching staff, and external agencies to ensure effective support and inclusion.
Interventions: Support includes social skills, emotional literacy, executive functioning, academic mentoring, and specialist input (e.g., physiotherapy, visual/hearing impairment support).
Monitoring: The impact of interventions is closely tracked through progress data, attendance, behaviour, and student, staff and Parent Voice, ensuring support is effective and responsive to individual needs.
Admissions and Transition
Transition Support: On entry to Year 7, we liaise with primary schools, visit students in their current settings, and invite families for tours and meetings with the SENDCo and Inclusion team. All new SEND students complete the strength and difficulty questionnaire to inform support planning.
EHCP Admissions: Pupils with Special Educational Needs who have an Education Health Care Plan (EHCP), supported by written evidence supplied by a recognised authority, will be admitted automatically where the school has been named by the Local Authority, in consultation with the school, on the EHCP for the child.
Communication and Engagement
Regular Updates: Progress and intervention updates, SEND parent coffee mornings and termly online Parent Hub meetings strengthen communication and collaboration with parents, carers and guardians, fostering positive home/school relationships built on trust.
Consultation: The SENDCo, inclusion team, Heads of Year and form tutors are available for consultation on request.
Statutory and National Context
National SEND Reforms: The SEND and Alternative Provision Improvement Plan (DfE) and recent Ofsted changes require schools to demonstrate inclusive practice, evidence-based interventions, and robust monitoring of SEND provision (2026, Schools White Pape, every school achieving and thriving).
Accountability: Schools are now held to higher standards for SEND, with greater scrutiny and support from Ofsted and Regional Improvement for Standards and Excellence (RISE) Teams.
Dr Smith, SENDCo, can be contacted initially through our school office at office@uptoncourtgrammar.org.uk and we welcome any questions or feedback.
Parent Hub Meetings – these meetings are scheduled via Teams on the last Wednesday of each term.

History of the School
In 2013, Upton Court Grammar School became the parent school to Upton Court Educational Trust, later re-named to Pioneer Educational Trust (2017). This incorporated Foxborough Primary School (2013) and Trevelyan Middle School (2016). The overall leadership of the Trust was held by: 2013 – 2017 – Mrs M Hernández Estrada, Executive Principal of Upton Court Educational Trust 2017 – 2018 – Mrs M Hernández Estrada, CEO of Pioneer Educational Trust 2018 – Present – Mrs A Spinks and Mr E Neighbour, Co-CEO’s of Pioneer Educational Trust
Having celebrated a hundred years of providing outstanding education to youngsters in Slough, the school re-launched itself building upon its past successes while looking forward into the 21st century. Supported by significant improvement to its facilities through a multi-million pound government investment, the school re-named itself to Upton Court Grammar School. It also became the parent school to the Pioneer Educational Trust, incorporating a local primary school (2013) and a Windsor Middle School (2016). Headteachers 2013 – 2017 Mrs M Hernández Estrada (continued as CEO of Pioneer Educational Trust) 2017 – Mr M Pritchard
The school reverted to its original name, Slough Grammar School as a Grant Maintained School, and later converted to Foundation School (2002), Trust School (2006), and Academy (2011). Headteachers 1988 – 2010 Mrs M Lenton 2010 – 2013 Mrs M Hernández Estrada (continued as Head of Upton Court Grammar School in 2013).
The girls and boys school merged in 1982, and became known as Upton Grammar School, after the Upton ward of Slough where Lascelles Road is located. Headteachers 1982 – 1988 Mr G Painter 1988 – 1993 Mrs M Lenton (continued as head of Slough Grammar School until 2010)
Having outgrown its premises, the School split into two and became Slough Grammar School for Boys and Slough High School for Girls. The boys moved immediately to Lascelles Road, but the girls remained at William Street for two more years until their new building in Twinches Lane was completed. Headteachers Boys 1936 – 1952 Mr E Rudland Clarke 1952 – 1966 Dr W R V Long 1966 – 1982 Mr G Painter (continued as head of Upton Grammar School until 1988) Girls 1936 – 1962 Miss J M Crawford 1962 – 1978 Miss G Owen 1978 – 1982 Miss P Reakes
Slough Secondary School was the first major co-educational selective school established in Slough (originally Buckinghamshire, now Berkshire), and occupied a building in William Street in the Town Centre. The William Street building was replaced by the tower block which is now the Slough Campus of Thames Valley University. Headteachers 1912 – 1925 Mr W Francis-Smith 1923 – 1925 Mr B Llewellyn (Acting) 1925 – 1936 Mr E Rudland Clarke (continued as head of Slough Grammar School for Boys until 1952)

Overview
At UCGS, Personal, Social, Citizenship, Health and Economic (PSCHE) education is delivered both through dedicated lessons and as part of our wider pastoral programme. Our PSCHE curriculum helps students become successful and engaged citizens, equipping them with the knowledge and skills they need to flourish. Through engaging, discussion-based teaching, we guide students in exploring a wide range of topics and developing the tools to thrive in school and beyond.
Our PSHCE programme helps students grow into successful and engaged citizens and prepares them to thrive as future global changemakers. Learning is sequenced across the year so that students develop the knowledge, skills and values needed to flourish as individuals, to work positively with others, to contribute to society, and to understand their role in the wider world.
Curriculum
Half Terms 1 & 2 – Intrapersonal Thriving
Students start the year by focusing on how to thrive intrapersonally. They explore their own identity, values, opinions and needs, developing confidence and resilience as they settle into secondary school and navigate new social and environmental contexts. Lessons address themes such as managing peer and media influence, mental health and wellbeing, safety, self-esteem, and respecting diversity (including racism and sexism). These foundations equip students to reflect on themselves, manage emotions, and make thoughtful decisions.
Half Term 3 – Interpersonal Thriving
Next, students build skills to thrive interpersonally, learning how to create positive, respectful relationships with friends, family, and their wider community. They consider how their words and actions affect others, discuss healthy friendships, peer pressure and decision making, and develop communication skills to work collaboratively. Understanding how to support others and interact constructively is essential for any changemaker who hopes to inspire and influence people.
Half Terms 4 & 5 – Societal Thriving
In spring and early summer, the focus moves to societal thriving. Students explore how life in Britain is shaped by its laws, government, and shared values. Topics include online safety, the UK legal system, local and national government, family and community life, and discussions about equality and inclusion. These sessions nurture an understanding of how society functions and how students can play an active role as informed, engaged citizens.
Half Term 6 – Global Thriving
To finish the year, students turn their attention to global thriving. They investigate diversity and cultural perspectives around the world, examine the work of international organisations such as the UN, and learn how change is driven globally — from historic movements like the suffragettes to modern campaigns. These lessons inspire students to think beyond their immediate environment, preparing them to make a meaningful impact as future global changemakers.
Relationships and Sex Education
At UCGS, Relationships and Sex Education (RSE) goes beyond biology to help students build self-esteem, responsibility, and the skills to form positive, caring, and healthy relationships. We promote self-respect, dignity, empathy, and an understanding of parental and social responsibilities.
RSE supports students’ spiritual, moral, cultural, mental, and physical development, preparing them for adult life. It equips young people to make informed, responsible decisions, providing guidance through their physical, emotional, and moral growth.
This policy outlines the RSE provision, covering human growth and reproduction, healthy relationships, and addressing issues like peer pressure, risk-taking behaviours, and relevant legal responsibilities. Our goal is to help students understand themselves and their values, empowering them to make the right choices.
